To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a human matrix metalloproteinase- 1 (MMP1) mutant, GVSK, can be conditionally activated by Ca2+ in vitro and in a rat model in vivo.
we have identified two mutations in the human MMP- 1 catalytic domain, Gly159 to Val and Ser208 to Lyr, that confer Ca2+-dependent regulation of MMP-1 in vitro.
we have generated an MMP-1 mutant that is conditionally active in vitro and in a tissue model of fibrosis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of conditionally active matrix metalloproteinases for therapeutic use in the treatment of fibrotic diseases.
developing new protein therapeutics that are regulated by physiological parameters.
understanding the molecular mechanisms by which MMP-1 is regulated by Ca2+.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the mutant protein GVSK has a Ca2+-regulated activity that can be exploited in vivo to control the degradation of collagen I.
the GVSK protein is unstable in vitro and in low Ca2+, and the enzyme inactivates rapidly.
the mutant MMP-1, which has been engineered to have calcium-sensitive activity, may be useful as a therapeutic agent for the treatment of fibrotic disorders.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the conditional activity of MMP1 as a function calcium may be an effect treatment for fibrotics diseases.

we have created a protein library amiable to physiological parameter-based protein screening, which has allowed us to identify a protein that can be regulated by a physiological variable, in our case calcium.
we have engineered a human matrix-remodelinng enzyme (human MMP-1) to be conditionally active.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the activity of MMP- 1 can be regulated by the presence or absence of calcium.
it is possible to engineer MMP-1 into an enzyme that has regulated activity in vitro and in the skin of living animals.

the conditional activity of MMPs as a function of physiological parameters may be an effective approach to treat fibrotic diseases, and we are developing a library of conditionally active MMPs for use as therapeutics.
